title: On Fairness of Task Arithmetic: The Role of Task Vectors
claim: Across demographic subgroups, the adaptation method (task addition vs. LoRA or full fine-tuning) shows no consistent fairness or accuracy pattern, with mixed small gains and losses.
layout: 2 rows by 3 columns of grouped bar charts, with accuracy, DPD and EOD columns, and rows labeled (a) gender and (b) race, with error bars
description: Six grouped bar charts in a 2x3 grid. The top row, labeled (a) Gender-based demographic subgroups, covers Men, Non-Binary, Other, Trans Men, Trans Unspecified, Trans Women and Women. The bottom row, labeled (b) Race-based demographic subgroups, covers Asian, Black, Latinx, Middle Eastern, Native American, Other, Pacific Islander and White. The columns are Accuracy, DPD and EOD. Each subgroup has three bars with black error bars: slate blue for FFT, mint green for LoRA, and orange for Task Addition. Legends sit inside each plot. Accuracy bars are nearly equal at about 0.8. The DPD and EOD bars vary by subgroup, and no method is consistently lowest. Rotated x-axis labels and the large bar clusters draw the eye first.
caption: LoRA and FFT vs. Task addition with the optimal coefficient for the training accuracy ($\lambda = 0.8$ for gender setting and $\lambda = 0.5$ for race setting) on group-wise accuracy, demographic parity difference (DPD, lower is fairer), and equalized odds difference (EOD, lower is fairer). Error bars denote the standard error across three seeds. Columns: group-wise accuracy, DPD, EOD. No consistent pattern emerges indicating that task addition systematically degrades subgroup fairness relative to LoRA or FFT. While some subgroups show improvements or comparable results under task addition, others exhibit small declines.
abstract: Model editing techniques, particularly task arithmetic with task vectors, offer an efficient alternative to full fine-tuning by enabling direct parameter updates through simple arithmetic operations. While this approach promises substantial computational savings, its impact on fairness has remained largely unexplored -- despite growing concern over biased outcomes in high-stakes applications such as hate speech detection. In this work, we present the first systematic study of group fairness in task arithmetic within this binary text and image classification regime, comparing it against full fine-tuning (FFT) and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA). We evaluate across multiple language models and datasets using standard group fairness metrics, including Demographic Parity and Equalized Odds. Our analysis shows that task vectors can be tuned to achieve competitive accuracy while reducing disparities, and that merging subgroup-specific task vectors provides a practical mechanism for steering fairness outcomes. We further provide a theoretical bound linking task vector scaling to fairness metrics, offering insight into the observed trade-offs. Together, these findings establish task arithmetic not only as a cost-efficient editing method but also as a fairness-aware alternative to existing adaptation techniques, within the standard group-fair classification setting, laying the groundwork for responsible deployment of large language models.
